351.title: Not my contest
351.hook: you can be unbeatable if you enter no contest where winning isn't up to you (Enchiridion 19)
351.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners notice when they start comparing themselves with others and decline to stake their peace on outcomes that depend on others.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was omen, a sign read as a warning. Your line was just a bird.

Late at night, thumb on the screen. An old classmate just bought a house. Someone's kid got into the program. A coworker is posting from a beach so blue it looks fake. Nobody announced a race. Nobody handed out numbers. And yet somehow you're running, and losing, at eleven forty on a Tuesday. Epictetus never saw a phone, but section nineteen of his handbook speaks straight to that race, and it opens with a claim that sounds like a boast: you can be unbeatable.
screen: `ELEVEN FORTY ON A TUESDAY.` → `A RACE NOBODY ANNOUNCED.` → `YOU CAN BE UNBEATABLE.`

segments.voice: You can be invincible, Epictetus says, if you never enter a contest where winning isn't up to you. The Greek for contest is agon: a match, a bout, a trial of strength. Then the trap. When you see someone honored above you, or powerful, or admired, he says, watch out that the impression doesn't carry you off into thinking they must be happy. That's the moment a person signs up for a contest without noticing: their house, their title, their beach, and suddenly you're competitors. If what's truly good lies in what's up to us, he says, then there's no room for envy or jealousy. You can't envy someone for something that was never the prize. And then the line: you yourself don't really want to be a general or a magistrate or a consul. You want to be free. And there's only one road to that: to care little for things not in our power. This isn't a refusal to try at anything. Train for the race, apply for the job, write the book. What Epictetus refuses is to stake your peace on the result, which depends on judges, timing and other people. The contest where winning is up to you is a different one: patience against your own temper, honesty against your own excuses. You can win that one every day. So when the scrolling starts a race, you can stand at the line, watch the runners go, and say: not my contest.

Picture a starting line and the race beginning without you, while you stay where you are and say inside: not my contest. Then name the contest that is yours today, being patient, being honest, finishing one thing well, and rest there.

Your line: stand at the line. Your own race is the one with no other runners. Day three hundred fifty-one, done.

352.title: The insult
352.hook: it isn't the insulter who harms you but your judgment that you're harmed (Enchiridion 20)
352.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism pause, even for a single breath, before replying to an insult, giving the first flash of anger time to cool.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was agon, the contest. Your line was stand at the line.

A man in the street kicks Socrates. His friends are outraged and want him to take the man to court. Socrates shrugs. If a donkey had kicked me, he asks, would I sue the donkey? The story is told in Diogenes Laertius' Lives of the Philosophers. Not everyone manages that shrug. Somebody cuts in front at the pharmacy and calls you something under their breath, and for the rest of the afternoon you're writing speeches to them in your head. Section twenty of the handbook asks where, exactly, the injury happened.
screen: `SOCRATES IS KICKED.` → `WOULD I SUE THE DONKEY?` → `WHERE DID THE INJURY HAPPEN?`

segments.voice: Remember, Epictetus says, that it isn't the one who abuses you or hits you who insults you. It's your judgment about them, that they've insulted you. The Greek verb is from hybris, outrage, the word behind our hubris. The outrage, he says, is completed inside. So when someone provokes you, know that it's your own judgment that has provoked you. That sounds like blaming the victim, and it's worth slowing down here. Epictetus isn't saying the person behaved well, or that you shouldn't defend yourself or others from real harm. He's talking about the second injury, the one that keeps going all afternoon: the speeches in your head. That part, he says, runs on your verdict, and it can be looked at. Then the tool. Try above all, he says, not to be carried off by the impression. If you once gain time and delay, you'll more easily master yourself. Time and delay. A breath. A count of three. Going to the window before answering the email. Seneca, writing a whole essay on anger, said much the same: delay is the greatest remedy for anger. It's one of the places where the Stoic writers agree closely. The first flash is fast and hot. Many people find that if they give it a few seconds, it often cools enough for them to choose. Not suppressing anything. Just one breath between the sting and the reply.

segments.voice: Remember a moment when someone said something that stung, and let it replay once: the heat rising, the reply forming. At the exact point where you would answer, stop, and take one slow breath in and out. Notice what's different on the other side of it; maybe the reply is the same, maybe it's softer, or unnecessary.
The insult. In Epictetus' handbook, completed not by the one who abuses you but by your judgment that you've been harmed, and loosened by a little delay. Today's word.
Your line: a breath before. The sting comes fast; the answer can come after. Until tomorrow.

353.title: Nothing to envy
353.hook: keep death and exile before your eyes daily, and you won't grasp or envy (Enchiridion 21)
353.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners briefly bring death or loss to mind each day, as a way of loosening envy and grasping rather than as a source of fear.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the insult, completed by your own judgment. Your line was a breath before.

Two words sit at the start of section twenty-one, and neither is cheerful: death and exile. It's a strange place to look for a cure for envy. Envy looks sideways, at a neighbor's new kitchen, a friend's easy promotion, the couple whose photos never seem to have a bad day. Epictetus points somewhere else entirely, and he asks for it every day, not once in a while. The note in the handbook is short and blunt, and the payoff he promises is an odd one.
screen: `DEATH AND EXILE.` → `ENVY LOOKS SIDEWAYS.` → `EVERY DAY, NOT ONCE IN A WHILE.`

segments.voice: Let death and exile, and everything that seems terrible, be before your eyes every day, Epictetus says, and death most of all. Then, he says, you'll never think anything low or petty, and you'll never want anything too much. Notice what he doesn't promise. Not that you'll be less afraid, or more cheerful. He promises a change in what you want. Here's how it works. Envy depends on a sense that the thing you envy is huge. Their promotion, their renovation, their perfect vacation. Set it in the light of death and it shrinks to its real size, not worthless, just the size of something that will be left behind. The Stoics weren't alone here. In Plato's Phaedo, Socrates calls philosophy a kind of practice for dying. The Latin phrase memento mori, remember you'll die, names the same habit. And the gentle part. This isn't meant to darken the day. Done gently, it can work the other way. The coffee tastes like coffee. The annoying coworker becomes a person who will also die, which is strangely tender. And envy, that tight, sour feeling, loosens, because in this light there's nothing to win. Everyone at the table, the one with the new car and the one with the old bike, is on the same short visit. If death feels too heavy today, start with exile: picture leaving behind everything you own. It does the same quiet work.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you envy, someone's house, job, body or ease, and gently widen the picture: fifty years from now, or a hundred, the house belongs to strangers, the job is a line in a story nobody tells, the person is gone, and so are you. Hold it without fear, the way you'd look at the sea. Then look back at the thing you envied, and see what size it is now.
Memento mori. Latin for remember you'll die; Epictetus' daily habit: keep death and exile before your eyes, and you'll want nothing too much. Today's word.
Your line: on the same short visit. In that light, there's nothing to win. That's day three hundred fifty-three.

354.title: Expect to be laughed at
354.hook: take up philosophy and some will mock you; hold to what seems best (Enchiridion 22)
354.howItsDone: Some people who take up a philosophical or spiritual practice keep it quietly, without explaining or showing off, and let teasing pass.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was memento mori, remember you'll die. Your line was on the same short visit.

A sibling rolls their eyes. A friend says, oh, so you're a philosopher now. A coworker catches you breathing at your desk and makes a joke about it. After almost a year of this practice, pausing before you answer, sitting for two minutes in the morning, saying a line under your breath at the stoplight, someone was bound to notice. Section twenty-two of the handbook has a line for this, and it could almost be your sibling talking. Epictetus warned his students to expect it.
screen: `A SIBLING ROLLS THEIR EYES.` → `OH, SO YOU'RE A PHILOSOPHER NOW.` → `EPICTETUS SAW IT COMING.`

segments.voice: If you want philosophy, section twenty-two says, get ready from the start to be laughed at. Many will mock you. They'll say: he's come back to us a philosopher all of a sudden. And: where did he get that superior look? The Greek for that look is ophrys, literally the eyebrow, the raised brow of someone who thinks they're above it all. And here Epictetus turns to his own students first. Don't put on that look, he says. The mockers may be rude, but don't hand them a reason. Instead, hold to what seems best to you, as someone posted to that place by God. The image is a soldier at a post, not showing off, just staying. Readers who don't share Epictetus' belief in God can still hear the shape of it: a commitment you keep quietly, because it's yours to keep. Then the two endings. If you stay with it, he says, the same people who laughed at first will come to admire you. But if you give in to them, you'll be laughed at twice. He might be too hopeful about the first; some people never stop teasing. But the second rings true: dropping a practice because of a joke rarely ends the joking. It just adds a new one. So: no raised eyebrow, no speeches about your new morning routine. Just keep doing it, kindly, and let the laughter be weather.

Hear the joke, and notice the urge to explain, or to quit, or to look superior. Let all three go, and see yourself just doing the practice, quietly, and carrying on with your day.

355.title: Keep your footing
355.hook: turn outward to please someone and you've lost your footing (Enchiridion 23)
355.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners notice when they are shaping their words to win someone's approval, and return to saying what they actually think, kindly.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was ophrys, the raised eyebrow. Your line was hold to it.

You're in a meeting and your manager floats an idea you think won't work. You open your mouth to say so. Then you see their face, hopeful, a little proud, and you hear yourself say: yeah, that could be great. Or you're at a party, someone makes a joke about a group of people, and you laugh along, a beat late, because everyone else did. Afterward there's a small wobble, as if the floor had tilted. Section twenty-three of the handbook is only a few lines long, and it names that wobble exactly.
screen: `YEAH, THAT COULD BE GREAT.` → `LAUGHING A BEAT LATE.` → `THE FLOOR TILTS.`

segments.voice: If it ever happens, Epictetus says, that you turn outward because you want to please someone, know that you've lost your footing. The Greek word is enstasis: a stance, a way of standing, a plan of life you've set yourself in. The moment you face outward to win approval, you've stepped off it. Kindness isn't the problem. Bringing a friend soup, choosing the restaurant your partner likes, laughing at a child's bad joke: those can all come from your own footing. The trouble is when the aim shifts from doing right to being liked, and you start bending your words to someone else's face. The remedy: be content, he says, in everything, simply to be a philosopher. And if you also want to seem one, seem one to yourself. That's enough. It's a strangely freeing sentence. You need one witness, and you already have them. Keeping your footing doesn't mean saying every harsh thing you think. In the meeting, it might sound like: I'm not sure that will work, can I say why? At the party, it might be not laughing, and changing the subject. Quiet, small, honest. People-pleasing can look like it buys peace. Epictetus thinks the price is higher than it looks. Each tilt toward someone's approval hands them a little of the ground you stand on. Keep it.

356.title: Faithful and modest
356.hook: you help your city not by holding office but by being trustworthy and self-respecting (Enchiridion 24)
356.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners measure their usefulness less by status or money than by being trustworthy and self-respecting in ordinary dealings.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was enstasis, your stance. Your line was keep my footing.

Down the hall lives the neighbor who signs for your packages and actually remembers to tell you. Who returns the ladder. Who says she'll water the plants while you're away, and you come home to plants that are alive. She doesn't sit on the city council. She'll never have a plaque. But the whole building runs a little better because she's in it. Section twenty-four of the handbook imagines a student who worries that a philosopher with no money and no office is useless to his friends and his city. Epictetus answers, and that neighbor is in the answer.
screen: `THE NEIGHBOR WHO SIGNS FOR PACKAGES.` → `NO OFFICE, NO PLAQUE.` → `IS A PHILOSOPHER USELESS?`

segments.voice: Don't let thoughts like this trouble you, Epictetus says: I'll live without honor, a nobody everywhere. Getting an office, being invited to a dinner, those aren't up to you. So how can missing them be your dishonor? You only need to be somebody in what's yours, and there you can be worth a great deal. But my friends will get no help from me, the student says. What help? Epictetus asks. Money? Roman citizenship? Who told you those were in your power? Show me how to get them while staying trustworthy and self-respecting and generous, and I'll get them. But if you ask me to lose my own good so you can have things that aren't truly good, see how unfair that is. And which would you rather have: money, or a faithful, self-respecting friend? But my country will get no help from me. What help? It won't get colonnades or public baths from you. Fine. It doesn't get shoes from the blacksmith either, or weapons from the shoemaker. It's enough if each does their own work. If you made one more citizen trustworthy and self-respecting, would that be no use? Faithful is pistos: trustworthy, the one whose word holds. Modest is aidemon: self-respecting, with a sense of shame in the good sense, the person who won't do what's beneath them. What place will you hold in the city, then? Whatever place you can hold while staying faithful and modest. Lose those trying to help, he says, and what use will you be, faithless and shameless?

357.title: The price of lettuce
357.hook: someone else got invited: they paid the price in flattery, and you kept your coin (Enchiridion 25)
357.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners, when passed over, ask what price the other person paid and remind themselves of what they kept by not paying it.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was pistos, faithful. Your line was each does their own work.

The group photo goes up and you're not in it, because you weren't invited. Or the promotion goes to the person who laughs at all the boss's jokes and stays for every after-work drink. Or the dinner party is next Saturday, and somehow your name didn't make the list. There's a sting, and right behind it a question: why them and not me? In the handbook, Epictetus answers with a trip to the market, to the vegetable stall, where a head of lettuce costs one small coin.
screen: `THE PHOTO YOU'RE NOT IN.` → `WHY THEM AND NOT ME?` → `A TRIP TO THE MARKET.`

segments.voice: Someone was preferred to you, Epictetus says, at a dinner, or in being greeted, or in being asked for advice. If those are good things, be glad for them. If they're bad, don't be sorry they didn't come to you. Then the market. How much is lettuce sold for? An obol, a small coin. Someone pays the obol and takes the lettuce. You don't pay, and you don't take it. Are you worse off than the buyer? He has the lettuce. You have the obol you didn't spend. So it is here, he says. You weren't invited to someone's dinner? You didn't pay the host what the dinner sells for. And the price is praise, and attention, and hanging around his doors, and putting up with his rudeness. If it's worth it to you, pay the price and go. But if you want the dinner without paying, you're being greedy and foolish. And you haven't come away with nothing. You didn't praise someone you didn't want to praise. You didn't put up with their insolence at the door. That's the coin in your pocket. It doesn't mean every invitation is bought with flattery; many are just friendship. But when someone gets ahead by paying a price you chose not to pay, notice the coin you kept. A look back at a week of steady footing: not my contest, the insult, nothing to envy, laughed at, keep your footing, faithful and modest, and the lettuce.
screen: `SOMEONE WAS PREFERRED TO YOU.` · `LETTUCE COSTS AN OBOL.` · `THE DINNER'S PRICE: PRAISE, ATTENTION.` · `THE COIN YOU KEPT.` · then, large: `I KEPT THE COIN.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing someone else got that you didn't, an invitation, a role, a seat at a table, and let the sting come. Then ask Epictetus' market question, what did it cost, and name the price honestly, if there was one: flattery, late nights, keeping quiet. Put your hand on your pocket and name the coin you kept: your time, your honesty, your evening.
Obol. The small coin that buys the lettuce in Epictetus' market lesson: everything has a price; if someone paid it and you didn't, they have the lettuce, and you have the coin. Today's word.
Your line: I kept the coin. Another week of steady footing, done. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 357 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHEN A NEIGHBOR'S CUP BREAKS.`
